analysis.one_liner: Bars doctors from billing Medicare for imaging, pathology, radiation therapy, and physical therapy they refer to their own in-office facilities.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, a vote, or action in either House committee and died at the end of the 113th Congress in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: Current law lets doctors refer Medicare patients for complex services — advanced imaging, anatomic pathology, radiation therapy, physical therapy — to facilities they own in their own offices, even though studies cited in the bill show this inflates volume and costs. The bill would close that loophole for those four service lines while keeping the exception for simple services actually performed during a routine office visit, and it would raise penalties for illegal self-referral billing. It died in committee without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers. By removing complex services from the in-office exception, the bill aims to eliminate the financial incentive for doctors to order unnecessary scans, pathology tests, radiation courses, and therapy sessions at facilities they own, which the bill's findings say cost Medicare hundreds of millions of dollars a year in excess services. Patients would also avoid care decisions driven by their doctor's ownership stake. Independent labs, imaging centers, and hospitals would gain referrals currently captured by physician-owned equipment.

how_it_helps.text: It closes the in-office ancillary services loophole for four service lines — anatomic pathology, radiation therapy, advanced diagnostic imaging, and physical therapy — so doctors who own those facilities cannot bill Medicare for referring their own patients to them.

It raises the civil money penalties for illegal self-referral billing from $15,000 to $25,000 per service and from $100,000 to $150,000 for circumvention schemes, and adds targeted compliance reviews of high-risk billing.

It preserves the exception for routine services actually performed during an office visit and for rural providers, and requires the savings to flow back through the physician fee schedule rather than being absorbed elsewhere.

analysis.who_pays: Physician practices that own or lease in-office imaging machines, pathology labs, radiation therapy equipment, or physical therapy operations would lose the Medicare revenue from referrals they control. Some patients who valued having these services coordinated in their doctor's office might face more referral steps.

drawbacks.text: Patients who value one-stop care could lose some convenience: the bill removes complex services from the exception even in cases where a physician's office does provide them competently in-house.

Some physician practices, including specialist groups, argue the in-office exception lets them coordinate and control quality of care directly, and closing it shifts that work to outside laboratories and imaging centers.

The bill grants the Secretary of Health and Human Services broad discretion to define which services count as 'specified non-ancillary services,' leaving the scope of the restriction to future regulation rather than the statute.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On the merits, the bill is strongly weighted toward the public and the program's finances: it targets a loophole that government studies show inflates Medicare spending, and the main drawback — losing in-office access to complex services — is small, since the evidence shows those services were rarely performed at the visit anyway. The bill's design also preserves the exception for routine services and rural providers. Its fatal weakness was political: physicians who profit from self-referral have a strong stake in the current rules, and the bill died quietly without ever being considered.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, sent to a Health subcommittee the next day, and then sat there untouched — no hearing, no vote, no floor action — until Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Jackie Speier introduced the bill on August 1, 2013, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees.
On August 2, 2013, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, where no further action was ever recorded.
No hearing, markup, or vote is listed in the bill's action history through the end of the 113th Congress on January 3, 2015.

The bill's own findings cited GAO and MedPAC studies showing self-referral drove hundreds of thousands of excess Medicare imaging and pathology services, costing Medicare over $100 million in imaging alone in 2010.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Physician practices that profit from referring Medicare patients to imaging, pathology, radiation therapy, and physical therapy services they own themselves are better off, because the restriction never took effect. Medicare's self-referral loophole remains open.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Self-referring physician practices; the loophole survives

for.name: Rep. Jackie Speier
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to close the Medicare self-referral loophole for complex in-office services.

for.name: Reps. Dina Titus and Jim McDermott
for.role: Original cosponsors, joined by 13 other House members (14 D, 1 R)

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral, sent it to the Health subcommittee on August 2, 2013, and never scheduled a hearing or markup.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no recorded action on it during the 113th Congress.

against.name: Self-referring physician groups (urology, oncology, and related specialty practices)
against.what_they_did: Historically opposed bills curbing the in-office self-referral exception, which protects revenue from in-office imaging, pathology, and radiation therapy for specialty practices.

sides.party_line_note: The cosponsor list was heavily Democratic (14 Democrats, 1 Republican), but the bill never advanced far enough for a roll-call vote to show how support actually split on the floor.

industries.industry: Physician-owned imaging, pathology, radiation therapy, and physical therapy operations
industries.note: The bill would cut off Medicare billing for services doctors refer to their own in-office facilities in these four lines, removing the financial incentive to order more scans, pathology reads, radiation courses, and therapy visits. Studies cited in the bill tie self-referral to hundreds of thousands of excess Medicare services each year.

industries.industry: Independent laboratories, imaging centers, and hospitals
industries.note: These providers compete with self-referring physician offices for the same Medicare work; banning self-referral would route referrals back to them. Patients' samples and scans would flow to outside facilities instead of the physician's own.辐射

The bill's stated purpose is to save Medicare billions of dollars by removing volume-inflating incentives, and it directs that resulting savings be reflected in the physician fee schedule. It imposes no new costs on beneficiaries, though curbing self-referral may shift some care to outside facilities.
